failure_summary.description: Selected weaker or stronger-looking claims without verifying which option was the strongest conclusion actually supported.
Lost exact theorem conditions, including a countability criterion and the exponent in an asymptotic.
Chose a nearby but incorrect congruence condition after speculating about the underlying classification.

patch.reasoning: Several failures persisted despite existing general cautions and topic-specific distinctions. A concise option-audit procedure makes those rules actionable: verify each candidate against the exact result, compare their logical strength, and avoid changing scope or precision based on speculation.

edits.target: Before choosing an option, identify the exact definition or theorem the question is testing. Parse every displayed expression literally, then compare the options’ hypotheses, quantifiers, exponents, endpoint spaces, and requested level of detail. Do not invent a theorem, exceptional case, or stronger conclusion from analogy or from a plausible-sounding citation. If you cannot verify a stronger claim, select only what the stated result supports.
edits.content: Before choosing, audit the options: rewrite each as its domain and quantifiers, hypotheses, conclusion, and strength; then compare the claims by implication. Verify the exact theorem or derivation before selecting the strongest claim it supports. An upper bound does not imply an asymptotic equivalence; a result for all cases must not be weakened because of a conjectured obstruction, and a result for a restricted class must not be generalized without proof. Keep equality, iff, endpoint, dimension, and parameter conditions literal. For algorithmic claims, include no-solution detection and preprocessing in the runtime, and read “finds” as “finds if a solution exists.” Do not use speculative neighboring results or imagined counterexamples as verification; stop after the audit identifies the strongest supported option.
